extracted.intended_audience: artists, students of art, and cultured citizens (including women of England); attendees of a public lecture
extracted.subtask_description: A Victorian lecture giving normative guidance on the moral duties of artists and of women (household and public roles), and on the relation of art to life, religion, and national welfare. It prescribes standards for artistic motive, craftsmanship, public responsibility, and the social importance of nature in education.

rubrics_metrics.name: Woman's household office
rubrics_metrics.description: A woman's personal work or duty, relating to her own home, is to secure its order, comfort, and loveliness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is presented as the primary domestic responsibility: maintaining order, providing comfort, and creating beauty within the household. It is the seed function which, when expanded, becomes her public duty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Woman's public duty (expanded household function)
rubrics_metrics.description: A woman's duty as a member of the commonwealth is to assist in the ordering, in the comforting, and in the beautiful adornment of the state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The private virtues exercised at home should be extended publicly: women should bring their capacities for order, consolation, and beauty into civic life, not confine them to private spheres.

rubrics_metrics.name: Man's public duty (parallel statement)
rubrics_metrics.description: A man's duty as a member of the commonwealth is to assist in the maintenance, in the advance, in the defence of the state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as a contrast to clarify roles: men's domestic role (maintenance/provision) expands into public service in defence and advance of the state; this sets a parallel framework for evaluating civic duties by gender in the lecture's argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature and landscape as essential schoolroom
rubrics_metrics.description: The land and natural scenes (mountains, bays, hills) are the proper schoolroom and play-ground for children and shape the national mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not industrialize or defile the countryside (the coal-shaft metaphor). Preserving gardens, bays, and mountains is necessary for children's moral and mental development; loss of natural environment impoverishes education and national character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve the country for future generations
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not turn the little garden of the country into furnace ground for present gain; such short-term exploitation harms children yet to come.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The evocative coal-shaft hypothetical warns against sacrificing the nation's natural beauty and health for increased income; it's a criterion for responsible stewardship and long-term thinking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Woman's use of power should be healing and guiding
rubrics_metrics.description: The love of power in woman should be directed to 'Power to heal, to redeem, to guide, and to guard' rather than 'Power to destroy.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Desire of power is not to be condemned if rightly directed; women should covet and exercise power that maintains justice and ministry of mercy, seeking queenly office with duty rather than mere precedence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lady/Lord titles imply public duties
rubrics_metrics.description: The title 'Lady' properly corresponds to 'bread-giver' and 'Lord' to 'maintainer of laws'; titles are only just if their holders perform the public offices they signify.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Women should claim titles only if they accept the responsibilities: feeding and serving the multitude (charity) and maintaining justice; nobility should be measured by beneficence, not mere precedence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Queenship as obligation, not mere honor
rubrics_metrics.description: Women are necessarily queens in many hearts; they should not be idle or careless queens grasping at majesty in small things while abdicating it in great ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The lecture urges active moral leadership: women must use their influence to check misrule and violence, to comfort and teach, and to occupy their public crown by service rather than vanity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Women responsible for restraining war and injustice
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no war or injustice for which women are not answerable—not because they provoked it, but because they have not hindered it; they are to choose men's causes and forbid them when there is none.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Women, through sympathy and moral imagination, are uniquely positioned to feel suffering and to lead or restrain men's passions; failure to act morally is culpable.

rubrics_metrics.name: The path of a good woman revives and leaves beauty behind
rubrics_metrics.description: A good woman's presence should not merely avoid destroying but should revive: 'the path of a good woman is indeed strewn with flowers; but they rise behind her steps, not before them.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Women should nurture and restore life—socially and morally—so that communities flourish because of their influence. The image functions as a standard for charitable, creative, and restorative action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arts must have noble motive
rubrics_metrics.description: The arts can never be right themselves unless their motive is right; they must be devoted to the proclamation of divine truth or of some unselfish patriotism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Art is morally and socially accountable: right motive (service of religion, patriotism, or unselfish national good) is fundamental to genuinely enduring and honorable art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skill (craft) is required alongside motive
rubrics_metrics.description: Fine motive alone does not make fine art; craftsmen must 'know their business'—motive without skill is ineffective and sometimes ludicrous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The lecture warns weak artists who plead noble motives: they must also acquire real technical ability (the 'hand' and 'head') to realize their intentions. Both aptitude and motive are required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artists bear a public trust and civic responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who possess great gifts must serve their nation faithfully with them; to abuse a great intellect is a treason to the people and a lasting curse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An artist's misuse of talent (serving vanity, pride, or lust) is morally culpable because a squandered or corrupted genius harms society permanently. This sets a standard of social accountability for creators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art prospers only when aligned with higher ends
rubrics_metrics.description: Art has not prospered unless its purpose was true—service of religion or unselfish patriotism—and it fails when it becomes minister to pride and lust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beyond motive, successful art historically accompanies sincere faith or national devotion; art that serves base ends will betray its trust at crises of culture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apathy is the chief barrier to art and virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: An intense apathy in people and artists prevents perception and virtue; the inability to feel or to care deeply for the ends of life obstructs true art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combating societal and individual apathy is essential: without lively moral feeling and attention, neither art nor ethical life can flourish. The lecture urges awakening of seriousness about life's ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art should reckon with life's mystery and immortality
rubrics_metrics.description: Art gains vital strength when motivated by a solemn faith in human immortality or in the advancing power of human nature; art that treats life as mere vanity lacks depth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The lecturer holds that enduring art proclaims or is consistent with belief in something beyond transient pleasures—this metaphysical seriousness is a criterion for the worth of artistic endeavour.
